title: Occasion, composition and title
short: Written in May-July 1802 as 'The Leech-Gatherer', from a meeting recorded by Dorothy Wordsworth in October 1800; published in Poems, in Two Volumes (1807).
body: On 3 October 1800 Dorothy's Grasmere journal describes an old man, bent almost double, born in the army to Scottish parents, who had lost nine of his ten children, had been badly hurt in a cart accident, and gathered leeches, which had grown scarce, and begged. Wordsworth drafted the poem between 3 and 9 May 1802 under the title 'The Leech-Gatherer' and revised it over the following weeks after criticism from Mary and Sara Hutchinson. It appeared in 1807 as 'Resolution and Independence'. The archive prints the 1807 text; later editions altered several lines (e.g. 'their pilgrimage' became 'life's pilgrimage'). The narrative moves the meeting from a Grasmere road to an open moor, and turns a charitable encounter into a crisis in the poet's own mind.

title: Stanza: rhyme royal with an alexandrine
short: Twenty-one seven-line stanzas rhyming ababbcc, the last line lengthened to six stresses (an alexandrine).
body: Wordsworth adapts rhyme royal (the stanza of Chaucer's Troilus) by stretching the final line, as in 'And all the air is fill'd with pleasant noise of waters'. The long line slows each stanza to a halt, a fitting rhythm for a poem about stillness and endurance. The form also links the poem to Chatterton, named in stanza 7, whose 'Excelente Balade of Charitie' (a poem about a poor pilgrim refused alms) may lie behind the choice of stanza, which would then be a tribute to the 'marvellous Boy', though the link is conjectural. The archaic, Spenserian flavour of the stanza suits the poem's later language of grace and admonishment.

title: Over his own sweet voice the Stock-dove broods
short: Wordsworth quoted this line in his 1815 Preface as an example of imaginative language: the dove seems to sit on its own note as on eggs.
body: The stock-dove is a wild pigeon of woods with a soft, repeated coo. In the 1815 Preface Wordsworth cites the line as an instance of the imaginative use of 'broods', which suggests how the bird dwells on and prolongs its note with quiet satisfaction, as if brooding over its own voice as over a nest. The comment shows how carefully he weighed the opening stanza's diction. The bird absorbed in its own music is also a quiet emblem of the self-delighting poet whom the poem will question.

title: The Hare and her mist
short: The hare's feet throw up spray from the wet ground, which glitters and 'runs with her': an image of creaturely joy.
body: 'Plashy' means wet, splashy, full of puddles. The hare running 'races in her mirth' is the emblem of unreflecting happiness, recalled in stanza 5 when the speaker compares himself to 'these blissful Creatures'. The glittering mist that accompanies the hare is a precise observation and also a figure of the transient radiance that surrounds joy; it is gone as soon as the hare stops.

title: I was a Traveller then upon the moor
short: The poem shifts from present to past tense: the speaker is recalling the morning, which turns the poem into a remembered crisis.
body: The first two stanzas are in the present ('now the sun is rising'); stanza 3 reveals they are a remembered scene. The 'Traveller' is the poet himself, on foot, a characteristic Wordsworthian figure of the wanderer. The setting is an upland moor; Wordsworth later said the state of mind came to him while crossing Barton Fell near Ullswater, whereas the old man had been met near Dove Cottage. 'My old remembrances went from me wholly' describes a forgetting of sorrows that will not last.

title: From joy to dejection
short: Extreme joy suddenly collapses into equal depression: the mind's swing is the poem's subject.
body: The stanza states a psychological law: 'As high as we have mounted in delight / In our dejection do we sink as low'. Wordsworth was writing in the weeks after Coleridge sent the verse letter that became 'Dejection: An Ode' (April 1802), and the two poems are in dialogue about joy, despondency and the poet's vocation. 'Dim sadness, & blind thoughts I knew not nor could name' describes depression without an object, the 'grief without a pang' of Coleridge's poem.

title: a happy Child of earth
short: The speaker likens himself to the skylark and hare: carefree like them, and as unprotected against the future.
body: The skylark and the hare are creatures that live in the present. The comparison is first a boast and then a fear: 'But there may come another day to me, / Solitude, pain of heart, distress, and poverty.' The line of abstract nouns, ending on the alexandrine, sounds like a list of the leech-gatherer's actual conditions, which the poet has not yet met. Compare Burns's ending to 'To a Mouse', where the creature is luckier than the man because 'the present only toucheth' it.

title: genial faith ... genial good
short: 'Genial' here means native, inborn, life-giving: the poet's natural trust that good things come without effort.
body: The older sense of 'genial' (Latin genialis, from genius, the inborn spirit, also connected with generation) is 'belonging to one's nature; productive, enlivening'. Milton's Samson says 'So much I feel my genial spirits droop', and Coleridge's 'Dejection' (1802) laments 'My genial spirits fail'. Wordsworth's repetition questions this optimism: the stanza turns to a sharp moral question about a man 'who for himself will take no heed at all', a self-accusation for the poet's carefree life.

title: Chatterton, the marvellous Boy
short: Thomas Chatterton (1752-1770), the Bristol prodigy who forged medieval 'Rowley' poems and died in poverty in London at seventeen.
body: Chatterton's 'Rowley' poems, purportedly by a fifteenth-century priest, were a sensation; he went to London to live by writing and died of arsenic poisoning in August 1770, generally believed to be suicide. For the Romantics he became the type of neglected genius. 'The sleepless Soul that perish'd in its pride' suggests both his restless energy and the pride of a self-made career. Wordsworth's stanza form may recall Chatterton's 'Balade of Charitie'.

title: Him who walk'd in glory and in joy / Behind his plough
short: Robert Burns (1759-1796), the ploughman poet, who died at thirty-seven in debt and ill health.
body: Burns was hailed in Henry Mackenzie's review of the Kilmarnock Poems (The Lounger, December 1786) as a 'heaven-taught ploughman', and the image of the poet singing at the plough stuck to him. Wordsworth admired him deeply and later wrote poems at his grave. Here Burns is the second example, after Chatterton, of a poet whose youthful 'glory' ended in misery. The juxtaposition makes the speaker's fear concrete: inspiration does not guarantee a living.

title: By our own spirits are we deified
short: Poets are made god-like by their own imaginative power, and that same power exposes them to despair and madness.
body: The line can be read in two ways: as a proud claim that poets raise themselves to divinity by their genius, or as a warning that self-deification is the root of the fall ('in the end despondency and madness'). The sequence 'gladness ... despondency and madness' may also glance at William Cowper and Christopher Smart, both poets of famous mental illness, though only Chatterton and Burns are named. Coleridge's crisis of 1802 is part of the context. Many critics have seen here the poem's central anxiety about the self-sufficient imagination.

title: peculiar grace ... A leading from above
short: Theological language: a special, unearned favour of God, a providential 'leading'.
body: 'Peculiar' means particular, singled out (Latin peculiaris, 'one's own'); in Protestant theology 'special' or 'peculiar' grace is God's favour shown to particular persons. Wordsworth hedges ('whether it were ... a something given'), but the poem frames the meeting as providential, and its ending is a prayer. The old man appears 'unawares', i.e. unexpectedly, as if sent. The language of grace and 'leading' prepares the reader to see the old man as a providential messenger, a reading the poem both invites and qualifies, since what he says is plain and practical.

title: untoward thoughts
short: Perverse, unruly thoughts, hard to manage; 'untoward' once meant stubborn, refractory.
body: The older sense of 'untoward' (literally 'not inclined towards') is 'awkward, perverse, unmanageable', rather than the modern 'unfortunate'. The phrase names the depressive 'fears and fancies' of stanzas 4-7 as something the poet has been struggling with ('had striven'), just before the encounter. The sense survives in phrases such as 'an untoward child', meaning a wayward one. The stanza's long periodic sentence ('Now, whether it were ... Yet it befel ... When ... And ...') delays the sight of the man, so that his sudden appearance ('unawares') has the effect of an apparition.

title: The stone and the sea-beast
short: A famous double simile: the old man is like a boulder that seems alive, which is like a sea-creature that seems like a rock.
body: In the 1815 Preface Wordsworth analysed this passage as the chief example of how the imagination confers, abstracts and modifies: the stone is given something of the power of life to bring it near the sea-beast, and the sea-beast loses some of its vitality to resemble the stone, and the combined image is then applied to the old man. The boulder 'couch'd on the bald top of an eminence' is a glacial erratic, whose presence prompts wonder 'by what means it could thither come'. The man thus seems half mineral, half animal, poised between life and death, as stanza 11 says outright.

title: a Sea-beast crawl'd forth
short: Perhaps a seal basking on a rock or sandbank: an alien, primeval creature at the edge of two elements.
body: The second term of the simile moves from mineral to animal and from moor to shore. The creature that has 'crawl'd forth' from the sea suggests something very ancient, even primordial, at the boundary of land and water; that boundary is echoed in the pond where the leech-gatherer works. Wordsworth's own commentary (1815 Preface) treats the sea-beast as the mediating image between the stone and the man.

title: not all alive nor dead ... pilgrimage
short: The old man seems suspended between life, sleep and death; his bent body makes his life a 'pilgrimage'.
body: Dorothy's journal recorded an old man 'almost double'. The verse makes his bent posture a figure: head and feet 'coming together in their pilgrimage', as if life's journey had curved back on itself. Later editions read 'life's pilgrimage', making the allegory explicit. The language of pain, 'rage / Of sickness' and 'more than human weight' prepares for the man's role as an image of endurance beyond ordinary strength.

title: moorish flood
short: A moorland pool: 'moorish' means belonging to a moor, and 'flood' any body of water.
body: Wordsworth's word has nothing to do with the Moors; it is the adjective from 'moor' (marshy upland). 'Flood' in older and poetic usage can mean a stream, pool or lake. The cloud simile that follows ('That heareth not the loud winds when they call; / And moveth altogether, if it move at all') extends the stillness: the old man moves, if at all, as a whole, like a cloud in still air.

title: conn'd ... As if he had been reading in a book
short: 'Conned' means studied, scanned attentively; the old man reads the pond as if it were a book.
body: 'Con' (Old English cunnian, 'to try, examine') means to study or learn by heart. The leech-gatherer looking for leeches in the muddy water appears to be reading, and the simile invites a symbolic reading: he reads nature as a text, as the poet would wish to. Critics have often taken the old man as a type of patient interpretation set against the poet's anxious fancy.

anchor: grave Livers do in Scotland use
title: grave Livers ... in Scotland
short: Serious, devout people in Scotland; Dorothy recorded that the man was of Scottish parents.
body: 'Livers' are those who live in a certain way: 'grave livers' are people of sober and religious life. The comparison to Scottish speech fits Dorothy's note that the old man was of Scottish parentage, and reflects the English view of Scottish Presbyterians as serious, Bible-reading people with dignified speech. 'Who give to God and Man their dues' recalls Christ's 'Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's; and unto God the things that are God's' (Matthew 22:21).

title: Leech-gathering
short: Leeches were collected from ponds and sold to doctors and apothecaries for bloodletting.
body: Medicinal leeches were in heavy demand in the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries, and wild stocks in Britain were depleted, which is why the old man says they 'have dwindled long by slow decay'. Gatherers often waded and let the leeches attach to their bare legs, so the work was 'hazardous and wearisome'. Dorothy's journal records the man's complaint that leeches had become scarce.

title: a Man from some far region sent
short: The old man takes on a visionary quality, as if sent to give the poet 'human strength, and strong admonishment'.
body: As the speaker stops hearing his words, the man becomes an apparition 'met with in a dream'. 'Admonishment' means warning or reproof. The figure of a strange messenger whom the speaker does not fully hear has been read as the poem's real crisis: the poet is so absorbed in his own fears that he cannot attend to the man. Lewis Carroll noticed this comedy and parodied it in the White Knight's song in Through the Looking-Glass (1871), where the narrator repeatedly fails to listen to an 'aged aged man'.

anchor: mighty Poets in their misery dead
title: mighty Poets in their misery dead
short: The fear of stanza 7 returns: the deaths of Chatterton and Burns and the possibility of a poet's ruin.
body: The stanza gathers the poem's anxieties into a single line of abstract nouns and then this line about the poets. 'The hope that is unwilling to be fed' is a hope that refuses nourishment, a depression that resists consolation. The repetition of the earlier fear shows that the first meeting did not cure it. The list, without main verbs, imitates the speaker's mind returning helplessly to the same anxieties. The irony is that the man beside him embodies a cure the speaker has not yet taken in.

anchor: My question eagerly did I renew
title: The repeated question
short: The poet asks the same question twice, not having heard the answer: a comic and revealing failure of attention.
body: 'How is it that you live, and what is it you do?' repeats the question of stanza 14 ('What kind of work is that which you pursue?'). The old man patiently repeats himself 'with a smile'. Critics have discussed whether the poem is aware of its narrator's self-absorption; Carroll's parody fastened on exactly this repetition. The answer, when it comes again, is plain fact: the leeches have dwindled, 'Yet still I persevere'.

title: Yet still I persevere
short: The leech-gatherer's simple statement of endurance is the 'resolution and independence' of the title.
body: The title's abstract nouns are embodied here: a man who goes on working although his resources are failing. The point of the poem is that the poet's fears ('Solitude, pain of heart, distress, and poverty') are the old man's actual condition, and he bears them with cheerfulness and dignity. The word 'persevere' has a theological ring as well (the 'perseverance of the saints').

anchor: the Leech-gatherer on the lonely moor
title: The ending
short: The poet laughs at himself and prays: he will remember the old man as a model of firmness.
body: 'I could have laugh'd myself to scorn' is self-mockery at the contrast between the poet's imagined troubles and the old man's 'firm mind'. The prayer, 'God ... be my help and stay secure', echoes the Psalms' language of God as stay and support (e.g. Psalm 18:18, 'the Lord was my stay'). Some readers find the resolution too easy, a moral tacked on; others see the restraint of the ending, which offers only a memory to be held on to, as true to the poem's understated piety.
